name: Baserow
tagline: The same grids, forms, formulas and API Baserow's cloud sells, from one container on your own server.

local.note: Everything answers at http://localhost:8175, which means this computer and nowhere else, so the colleague you wanted in the table cannot open it and neither can your phone.

quote.text: Runs a Postgres database and Redis server by default internally and stores all data in the /baserow/data folder inside the container.

citations.claim: The all-in-one image upstream calls the recommended way to run Baserow keeps a PostgreSQL and a Redis inside the same container and stores everything under /baserow/data, which is why this install runs no separate database service.
SECRET_KEY and BASEROW_JWT_SIGNING_KEY are generated by the image into /baserow/data if they are not supplied from outside, so supplying them is what puts them in a file the backup carries.
Upstream's own deployment guide sets the health check for this image to port 80 and /api/_health/, and asks for a 900-second grace period to cover the first-time migrations.
The first user ever created on a Baserow instance is given staff rights, which is what makes that account the administrator.
Baserow's own admin settings describe the default plainly: any user visiting your Baserow domain can sign up for a new account until an admin turns that off.

whatYouSignUpFor: Same company, same product, sanctioned path. Baserow B.V. publishes the image, writes the install docs and sells the hosting, so this is not a lookalike. The LICENSE file splits the tree, which is why GitHub reports no single licence: the core is MIT Expat, the premium/ and enterprise/ directories carry their own separate licences, and docs/ is CC BY-SA. The free install you get here has grid, form and gallery views, formulas, linked tables, the REST API and no cap on rows or users. Kanban, calendar, timeline and survey views, personal views, row comments and the dashboard widgets are premium. Role-based permissions, field and view permissions, snapshots, audit logs, custom roles, XML and JSON and Excel export, SSO and secure file serving are advanced or enterprise. No setting turns any of them on; they want a licence key from the same company.

Four gigabytes, for one container. The all-in-one image runs a PostgreSQL 15, a Redis, the Django backend, the Nuxt web frontend and a Caddy of its own under one supervisor, so what looks like a single-service install is five processes sharing a memory budget. The first boot runs every migration and imports the built-in templates, which takes minutes rather than seconds, and the cheapest VPS tier will not do.

The administrator account is a race you have to win. Baserow creates the first account anyone submits and gives it staff rights, and new signups stay open until an admin turns them off in Admin settings. The install closes that window by making you claim the account at a stop and then asserting the toggle is off, but between the container answering and you finishing the form, the offer is public.

You own the backups, they need the container stopped, and they are not portable. Everything lives in one directory holding a live PostgreSQL cluster, so the archive is taken with five processes stopped and restores into this same image and this same PostgreSQL major version, not into a database you install elsewhere. The same archive carries .env, which is the only copy of the two keys that sign sessions and API tokens.

No mail means no invitations and no password resets. The core loop works without SMTP, which is why this install skips it, but the day you add a second person you either configure mail or create the account by hand, and a forgotten administrator password has no reset link.
